feedback_history.patient_message:
You're absolutely right. And that's the knot in my gut that won't let me breathe.

If I quit this job, we lose our mortgage payment buffer. We might even have to move into a smaller place or take out a loan just to keep the roof over our heads. My fiancee is already stressed about money; adding the mental load of *everything*—the house, the kids, the bills, the cooking, the cleaning, the constant vigilance for safety and needs—on top of his own depression... it feels like asking him to carry a mountain while he's already carrying one himself.

I've been trying to picture myself as a stay-at-home mom for years, but every time I close my eyes, I see the version of me who is screaming at 3 AM because there's no one else to help, or worse, snapping at them because I'm so drained I can barely lift a cup of coffee. That
feedback_history.therapist_response: I'm not sure I'm ready to make that decision.
feedback_history.feedback:
Validate the patient's exhaustion and acknowledge that her fear of snapping at her children is a rational response to burnout, not a character flaw.
Gently explore whether she has been able to eat or drink recently, linking her physical symptoms (knot in gut, fatigue) directly to her current stress level.
Refrain from pushing for an immediate decision on quitting; instead, focus on stabilizing her somatic state before discussing the financial implications further.

feedback_history.patient_message:
You're right. That image is exactly what I'm terrified of giving them.

I don't want my six-year-old to grow up watching their mom scream at a stranger on Zoom because she's too tired to say hello, or crying in the shower after dropping dinner so it burns the kids' lunch. I don't want them to see me collapse onto the floor and just... stop existing until morning. They are already sensing that something is wrong; they're picking up on the tension between us, the way my fiancee shuts down, and the way I snap at them when I have zero energy left.

If I stay home full-time without a break, the only thing that might come out of that house isn't love—it's resentment. And if I end up resenting *them* for needing me so much, or resenting myself for failing to provide the stability they deserve... that would be the real tragedy.

But here's the
feedback_history.therapist_response: You can't do your best when you're already so exhausted.

feedback_history.patient_message:
That makes sense. It's not a decision you can just "make" like turning off a light switch. It feels more like... trying to hold your breath underwater while holding two heavy bricks in each hand and wondering if you'll drown before you even get to the surface.

I feel like I'm stuck between two fires: one is the fire of my own sanity burning down, and the other is the fear that if I put out my own fire, the kids will freeze too. Or worse, they'll learn that when Mom gets tired, she stops being there entirely.

It's so hard to imagine stepping back into that role without the safety net of the job, especially when the house feels so fragile right now. Every time I think about it, I see the mortgage bill looming, or the grocery list getting longer, or my fiancee looking at me with those sad eyes that say, *"You're doing your best, honey."* And
feedback_history.therapist_response: And the kids know you're worried about them, but they just don't know that you're worried about yourself.
feedback_history.feedback:
Validate the patient's metaphor of 'two fires' to acknowledge the intense conflict between self-preservation and parental presence.
Gently probe for physical manifestations of this exhaustion, specifically asking if they are experiencing psychomotor changes like restlessness or slowed movement due to the stress.
Reframe the 'safety net' concept by suggesting that a functioning parent is actually a prerequisite for their own safety and stability.
